```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
```

## Introduction

The `cars` data set records the speed of `r nrow(cars)` cars and the distance
each took to stop. The measurements were made in the 1920s, so the speeds are
in miles per hour and the distances in feet.

## Summary statistics

```{r summary-stats, echo=TRUE}
cars %>%
  summarise(
    mean_speed = mean(speed),
    mean_dist  = mean(dist),
    max_dist   = max(dist)
  )
```

| Statistic | Speed (mph) | Distance (ft) |
|-----------|------------:|--------------:|
| Minimum   |           4 |             2 |
| Median    |          15 |            36 |
| Mean      |        15.4 |          42.98 |
| Maximum   |          25 |           120 |

## Speed and distance

```{r plot, fig.cap="Stopping distance against speed, with a quadratic fit.", fig.width=6, fig.height=4}
ggplot(cars, aes(speed, dist)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ poly(x, 2), se = TRUE) +
  labs(x = "Speed (mph)", y = "Stopping distance (ft)")
```

Physics predicts that braking distance grows with the square of speed,
$d \propto v^2$, while reaction distance grows linearly. A quadratic model
fits well:

```{r model}
fit <- lm(dist ~ speed + I(speed^2), data = cars)
summary(fit)$r.squared
```

The model explains `r round(summary(fit)$r.squared * 100)`% of the variance.

## Conclusion

> Stopping distance roughly quadruples when speed doubles.

Session details are recorded below for reproducibility.

```{r session, echo=FALSE}
sessionInfo()
```
